title: Project planning and scheduling
summary: PERT and CPM are the core, and two formulas carry most of the numerical questions: t_e equals (t_o plus 4t_m plus t_p) over 6, and sigma equals (t_p minus t_o) over 6 — note that sigma depends only on the two EXTREMES, not on the most likely value. For crashing, the procedure matters more than the arithmetic: crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope, then RECOMPUTE, because the critical path may change. And keep crashing (costs money) apart from fast tracking (costs risk) and from the resource techniques.

sections.heading: Project planning and the work breakdown structure
sections.body:
**A project** is a **temporary endeavour** with a **defined objective**, a **definite beginning and end**, **unique** deliverables, and **limited resources**. Those characteristics distinguish it from ongoing operations, and they are what make it need planning as a separate discipline.

**The project life cycle:**

> **Conception → Feasibility → Planning and design → Implementation (execution) → Commissioning → Operation → Closure**

**The distribution of influence and cost over that cycle is the most useful thing to understand about it:**

| Stage | Ability to influence the outcome | Cost incurred |
|---|---|---|
| **Conception and feasibility** | **HIGHEST** | **Lowest** |
| Planning and design | High | Low |
| **Implementation** | **Low** | **Highest** |
| Operation | Very low | Recurring |

> **The ability to influence cost and quality is greatest at the very beginning, when almost nothing has been spent — and least during construction, when almost everything is being spent.**

That is why effort at the **planning and design stage** is so disproportionately valuable, and why a decision to "save time by starting on site" almost always costs more than it saves.

**The Work Breakdown Structure (WBS):**

> A **HIERARCHICAL DECOMPOSITION of the total project SCOPE into manageable WORK PACKAGES.**

It proceeds from the project, through **deliverables and sub-deliverables**, to **work packages** small enough to be estimated, assigned, scheduled and controlled — typically representing 8 to 80 hours of work, or one reporting period.

**The WBS comes FIRST**, before the schedule, and this is examined:

| Derived from the WBS | How |
|---|---|
| **Activity list and network** | Each work package decomposed into activities |
| **Cost estimate** | Costed package by package, then rolled up |
| **Resource plan** | Resources assigned per package |
| **Responsibility assignment matrix** | Who owns each package |
| **Progress measurement / earned value** | Progress measured **against packages**, not against vague percentages |
| **Risk register** | Risks identified per package |

**The WBS answers "WHAT WORK EXISTS"; the network answers "IN WHAT ORDER".** They are different questions, and a bar chart or network built without a WBS invariably omits work — because nothing forced the planner to enumerate the scope systematically.

**The 100% rule** governs its construction: the WBS must include **100% of the work** defined by the scope, and **nothing outside it**. Each level's children must sum exactly to their parent.

**Planning tools, in order of information content:**

| Tool | Shows | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Bar (Gantt) chart** | Activity **durations against a calendar** | **Does NOT show DEPENDENCIES** — so it cannot identify a critical path |
| **Milestone chart** | Key dates only | No detail |
| **Linked bar chart** | Durations plus some links | Partial |
| **Network (CPM/PERT)** | **Logical dependencies** and the **critical path** | Less immediately readable |
| **Line of balance** | Repetitive work (housing, pipelines) | Specialised |
| **Time–location (time–chainage) chart** | **Linear projects** — roads, tunnels, pipelines | Specialised |

**The bar chart's inability to show dependencies is its fundamental limitation**, and it is why the network methods were developed: without knowing what delays what, a planner cannot tell which activities matter. Modern software resolves this by **drawing the bar chart FROM the network logic**, giving the readability of the one and the analysis of the other — which is why a modern programme looks like a bar chart but behaves like a network.

**Time–location charts** deserve note for civil engineering: on a **road, tunnel or pipeline**, plotting **chainage against time** shows at a glance where each gang is working, whether two activities will clash in space, and what the rate of progress is. A conventional bar chart cannot show that a paving gang and an earthwork gang will meet at chainage 12 km in March.

sections.heading: Network analysis — CPM
sections.body:
**Network conventions (activity-on-arrow):**

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Activity (arrow)** | A task **consuming time and resources** |
| **Event (node)** | A **point in time** — the start or completion of activities; consumes nothing |
| **Dummy activity (dashed arrow)** | **Zero duration**; shows a **dependency** only, or separates two activities sharing the same start and end events |

**Rules for a valid network:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| **One start event and one end event** | The project has one beginning and one end |
| **No LOOPING** | An activity cannot depend on its own successor — logically impossible |
| **No DANGLING** | Every activity must connect to the end event; a dangling activity has no successor |
| Events numbered so that **head number > tail number** | Fulkerson's rule; permits systematic computation |
| No two activities may have the **same pair of events** | Hence the **dummy** |

**Activity-on-node (precedence)** networks are now more common in software: activities are the **boxes** and arrows show dependencies, which avoids dummies entirely and allows four relationship types — **finish-to-start (the usual), start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish** — plus **lead and lag** times.

**The forward and backward pass:**

| Pass | Computes | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD** (left to right) | **Earliest** times: EST, EFT | **EFT = EST + duration**; at a merge, take the **LATEST** of the incoming EFTs |
| **BACKWARD** (right to left) | **Latest** times: LST, LFT | **LST = LFT − duration**; at a burst, take the **EARLIEST** of the outgoing LSTs |

**Take the LATEST on the forward pass and the EARLIEST on the backward pass** — the rule most often inverted, and the reason is logical: an activity cannot start until **all** its predecessors are complete (hence the latest), and must finish in time for **all** its successors to start on schedule (hence the earliest).

**Float (slack):**

| Float | Definition | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Total float** | **LST − EST** = LFT − EFT | Delay possible **without delaying the PROJECT** |
| **Free float** | EST of the following activity − EFT of this one | Delay possible **without delaying any SUCCESSOR** |
| **Independent float** | Free float less the predecessor's total float | Delay possible without affecting **either** neighbour |
| Interfering float | Total float − free float | — |

> **Total float ≥ free float ≥ independent float**, and independent float can be **negative** (taken as zero).

**The critical path:**

> The **LONGEST path** through the network, and therefore the one that **determines the PROJECT DURATION**. Its activities have **ZERO total float**.

**Two consequences follow, and both are examinable:**

1. **Delaying a critical activity delays the whole project**, day for day.
2. **Shortening a non-critical activity achieves NOTHING** — it has float, so the project duration is unchanged.

The second is why **crashing a non-critical activity is wasted money**, and why the critical path must be identified before any acceleration is attempted.

**A network may have MORE THAN ONE critical path**, and as activities are shortened, **paths that were near-critical become critical** — which is the point that makes crashing an iterative process rather than a single calculation.

**Near-critical paths** deserve attention in practice: a path with only two or three days of float is nearly as dangerous as the critical path itself, because any small delay makes it critical. A programme that reports only the critical path conceals that risk, which is why float distribution across the network is worth examining.

sections.heading: PERT and probabilistic scheduling
sections.body:
**PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique)** treats activity durations as **uncertain**, using a **three-point estimate**:

| Estimate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **t_o — optimistic** | The shortest time, if everything goes well |
| **t_m — most likely (modal)** | The time under normal conditions |
| **t_p — pessimistic** | The longest time, if things go badly |

**The activity duration is modelled by a BETA distribution**, giving:

> **Expected time t_e = (t_o + 4 t_m + t_p) / 6**
> **Standard deviation σ = (t_p − t_o) / 6**
> **Variance σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

**The most examined property:**

> **σ depends ONLY on the two EXTREMES (t_o and t_p). The most likely time t_m affects the EXPECTED time but NOT the standard deviation.**

So an option giving **(t_p − t_m)/6** for σ is wrong, and one giving **(t_p + t_o)/6** cannot be a measure of spread at all, since it **adds** rather than subtracts. Both appear as distractors.

The **6** in the denominator comes from the assumption that the range **t_o to t_p spans approximately six standard deviations** — that is, it covers essentially the whole distribution.

**Probability of completion — the whole reason PERT exists:**

1. Compute **t_e** for every activity and find the **critical path** in the usual way.
2. **Sum the VARIANCES of the activities on the critical path** — **variances add, standard deviations do NOT**.
3. **σ_project = √(Σσ²)**
4. For a target date **T**, compute the standard normal deviate:

> **Z = (T − T_e) / σ_project**

5. Read the probability from the **standard normal table**.

**Adding variances rather than standard deviations** is the step most often got wrong, and it follows from the statistics of independent random variables: the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances.

**Why this matters:** it lets a manager say **"we have an 85% chance of finishing by June"** rather than quoting a single bare date — which is a far more honest representation of a project whose durations are genuinely uncertain. A single-point date implies a certainty that does not exist.

**Note the symmetry results**: at **T = T_e**, Z = 0 and the probability is **50%** — a project has only a fifty-fifty chance of meeting its own expected duration, which surprises people and is worth stating.

**CPM and PERT compared:**

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Durations** | **DETERMINISTIC** — one estimate | **PROBABILISTIC** — three estimates |
| **Orientation** | **ACTIVITY**-oriented | **EVENT**-oriented |
| Origin | **Construction and maintenance** (DuPont, 1957) | **Research and development** (US Navy Polaris, 1958) |
| **Suits** | **REPETITIVE** work, where durations are known from experience — **construction** | **NOVEL** work, where durations are uncertain — research, development |
| **Cost** | Handles the **time–cost trade-off (crashing)** | Time only, in its original form |
| Output | A date | A **probability distribution** of dates |

**PERT's known limitation**, which is examinable:

> PERT sums the variances of the **CRITICAL PATH ONLY**. A **NEAR-CRITICAL path with HIGH variance can easily overtake it**, so the computed probability of on-time completion is **OPTIMISTIC** — sometimes substantially.

**Monte Carlo simulation** addresses this by **sampling all paths** thousands of times and building the true distribution of completion dates. It is what modern risk-analysis software does, and it routinely shows a project's realistic completion date to be later than PERT suggests.

**In practice the two methods have merged**: planning software computes network logic with deterministic durations, displays the result as a bar chart, and offers probabilistic simulation as an option. The distinction survives chiefly in examinations and in the vocabulary.

sections.heading: Time–cost trade-off, resources and control
sections.body:
**Crashing** is the deliberate shortening of activity durations by **adding resources at extra cost** — overtime, extra crews, additional plant, a faster method, or expedited materials.

**The two cost streams pull in opposite directions**, and that is the whole basis of the analysis:

| Cost | Behaviour as the duration is SHORTENED |
|---|---|
| **DIRECT cost** (labour, plant, material) | **RISES** — crashing is inefficient |
| **INDIRECT cost** (overheads, supervision, site establishment, financing, insurance) | **FALLS** — there are fewer days to pay for |
| **TOTAL cost** | **Falls, then rises — a MINIMUM exists** |

> **The duration at which total cost is minimised is the OPTIMUM DURATION.**

Shortening beyond it costs more than it saves; lengthening beyond it also costs more, through indirect cost. Finding that minimum is the object of the exercise.

**The cost slope** is the key quantity:

> **Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − crash duration)**

— that is, the **extra cost per day saved** on that activity.

**The procedure:**

1. Identify the **CRITICAL PATH** — only critical activities can shorten the project.
2. Among the critical activities, **crash the one with the LOWEST cost slope** first (the cheapest day to buy).
3. Crash it by one time unit, or to its crash limit.
4. **RECOMPUTE the network** — **the critical path may have CHANGED**.
5. Repeat until the target duration is reached, or until the **total cost begins to rise**.

**Step 4 is where the method is most often applied wrongly.** As a critical activity is shortened, a **previously non-critical path may become critical**. Once two paths are critical, **BOTH must be crashed simultaneously** to gain a further day — so the cost per day saved **rises in steps**, and eventually exceeds the indirect cost saving. That step-wise rise is exactly why the total cost curve has a minimum.

**A worked illustration of the logic:** with an indirect cost of Rs 10,000 per day, it is worth crashing while the cost slope is **below** Rs 10,000/day and not worth it above. Once the cheapest remaining option costs Rs 12,000/day, the optimum has been passed.

**Crashing, fast tracking and the resource techniques — four things routinely confused:**

| Technique | Constraint | Duration | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CRASHING** | **TIME** — shorten it | **REDUCED** | **Extra COST** |
| **FAST TRACKING** | Time | **REDUCED** | **Extra RISK** — activities normally sequential are **overlapped**, so rework is possible if the earlier one changes |
| **RESOURCE LEVELLING** | **RESOURCES are FIXED** (a limit cannot be exceeded) | **May be EXTENDED** | — |
| **RESOURCE SMOOTHING** | **DURATION is FIXED** | **UNCHANGED** | Activities shifted **within their FLOAT** to even out the resource profile |

**Crashing costs money; fast tracking costs risk** — that is the distinction to hold. And **levelling may extend the project while smoothing may not**, which is the distinction between the two resource techniques.

**Resource management** more broadly:

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Resource aggregation** | Summing the resource requirement over time — the **resource histogram** |
| **Resource smoothing** | Removing the peaks and troughs, using float |
| **Resource levelling** | Rescheduling to respect a **hard resource limit** |
| **Resource-constrained scheduling** | Scheduling where resources, not logic, govern |

**Why an even resource profile matters**: a histogram with sharp peaks means **hiring and releasing labour repeatedly**, which is expensive, disruptive and bad for quality and safety. Smoothing within float achieves a steadier profile **at no cost in duration**, which is why it is done first, before considering levelling.

**Project monitoring and control — EARNED VALUE:**

| Measure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PV — Planned Value** (BCWS) | The budgeted cost of the work **scheduled** to date |
| **EV — Earned Value** (BCWP) | The budgeted cost of the work **actually performed** to date |
| **AC — Actual Cost** (ACWP) | The **actual cost** of the work performed |

**The variances and indices:**

> **Cost variance CV = EV − AC** · **Schedule variance SV = EV − PV**
> **Cost Performance Index CPI = EV / AC** · **Schedule Performance Index SPI = EV / PV**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CPI or SPI > 1** | **Better** than plan |
| **= 1** | On plan |
| **< 1** | **Worse** than plan |
| **Negative variance** | Behind or over |

**Forecasts:**

> **EAC (Estimate At Completion) = BAC / CPI** — assuming the current cost performance continues
> **ETC (Estimate To Complete) = EAC − AC**

**Earned value's real contribution** is that it **separates the cost and schedule questions**, which a simple cost-against-budget comparison confuses. A project that has spent less than budgeted might be **economical or merely behind schedule** — and only by comparing what has actually been **earned** can the two be distinguished. That is why EV is the standard, and why it requires a **WBS with measurable work packages** to work at all.

**Other control tools:**

| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| **Updated network and bar chart** | Re-analysing with actual progress |
| **S-curve** | Cumulative cost or progress against time |
| **Milestone tracking** | Key dates |
| **Progress photographs and reports** | Evidence |
| **Look-ahead programmes** (2–6 weeks) | Short-term coordination on site |

**Updating is the discipline that makes any of it useful.** A programme prepared at the start and never updated becomes a work of fiction within weeks; one updated regularly with actual progress **shows the effect of a delay before it becomes irrecoverable**, which is the entire purpose of scheduling. The question a programme should answer is not "what did we plan?" but **"given where we now are, when will we finish, and what must change?"**

formulas.label: PERT three-point estimate
formulas.note: σ depends ONLY on the two extremes. t_m affects the expected time but NOT the standard deviation.

formulas.label: Probability of completion
formulas.expression: σ_project = √(Σσ² of critical path activities) ;   Z = (T − T_e)/σ_project
formulas.note: VARIANCES add, standard deviations do not. At T = T_e the probability is only 50%.

formulas.label: Forward and backward pass
formulas.expression: Forward: EFT = EST + d, take the LATEST at a merge. Backward: LST = LFT − d, take the EARLIEST at a burst.
formulas.note: The rule most often inverted. An activity waits for all predecessors, and must not delay any successor.

formulas.label: Float
formulas.expression: Total float = LST − EST ;   free float = EST(next) − EFT ;   total ≥ free ≥ independent
formulas.note: Critical activities have ZERO total float. Shortening a non-critical activity achieves nothing.

formulas.label: Cost slope
formulas.expression: cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal duration − crash duration)
formulas.note: The extra cost per day saved. Crash the CRITICAL activity with the LOWEST slope first, then RECOMPUTE.

formulas.label: Optimum duration
formulas.expression: Where TOTAL cost (direct rising + indirect falling) is a MINIMUM
formulas.note: Crash while the cost slope is below the daily indirect cost saving, and stop when it exceeds it.

formulas.label: Crashing versus fast tracking versus resource techniques
formulas.expression: CRASHING costs money. FAST TRACKING costs risk. LEVELLING may extend the duration. SMOOTHING keeps it fixed, shifting within float.
formulas.note: Four distinct techniques, routinely confused in questions.

formulas.label: Earned value
formulas.expression: CV = EV − AC ; SV = EV − PV ; CPI = EV/AC ; SPI = EV/PV ; EAC = BAC/CPI
formulas.note: Below 1 is bad for both indices. EV separates the cost question from the schedule question.

formulas.label: Network validity rules
formulas.expression: One start and one end event ; NO LOOPING ; NO DANGLING ; head number > tail number ; a dummy where two activities share both events
formulas.note: A dummy has zero duration and shows dependency only.
